name: Sheguiandah First Nation (Anishinabek Nation)
physical: The community offers a Health Centre that is both a medical clinic and an administration office for health and wellness. The Health Centre includes programs ranging from Community Wellness, Family Well-Being and Traditional Life-Styles, and Medical Transportation and health clinics are an important part of the Health Centre. It also offers Diabetes education/support programs.
mental: The community offers Family Well-being, which fosters support for families through well-being and mental health. The community also hosts a Mobile Mental Health & Addictions Clinic, which offers improving access to mental health and addictions care for people who live in the District of Manitoulin.
spiritual: The community offers an Elders Program with activities that include traditional teachings and ceremony. The community also offers Traditional & Life skills programming through the Health Centre, which focuses on traditions and culture and includes harvesting, teachings and land-based activities. The community also hosted Traditional Healer Arrole Lawrence through the Health Centre.
emotional: The community offers Family Well-being, which supports families through well-being and mental health. The community also offers Community Wellness Promoter, which  promotes Healing and Wellness, provides referrals for food security/mental health support, and facilitates programming that enhances the lives of community members.
survivors: The Elders Program is a community support program designed to provide community driven support services to elders and seniors and that is supervised by the Health Manager  and delivered by the Elders Coordinator.
youth: The community offers Early Years – Binojiinh Kinomaage-Gamik for children ages 0–6 years. Services include parent/child socializing, daily programming, nutrition programming, traditional programming, outdoor activities and excursions. The community also offers Education services through K-12, Post-Secondary Education, Special Education (K-12), and Adult Learning. K-12 monitors attendance and student progress, while Special Education includes after-school programs and specialized tutoring. The Health Centre also offers Right to Play Community Mentor, which is aimed at the youth of SFN and it creates a network of support for children and youth through programming.

By positioning survivors as mentors and cultural anchors, KGCFS facilitates the transmission of traditional knowledge through several key resources: 

Intergenerational Mentorship: Survivors can be matched with youth in care through the Match and Mentorship with an Elder program, providing direct one-on-one connection for cultural guidance.

Youth and Elders Cultural Gatherings: KGCFS hosts specific events, such as the Youth and Elders Cultural Gatherings, designed to nurture valuable connections through keynote speakers, interactive activities, and shared traditional teachings.

Land-Based Cultural Hubs: The new Enji-maajiigawat Mina-waadiziwin hub in Sudbury provides a physical space for survivors to lead workshops in sweat lodges, gardens, and teepees, helping youth reconnect with their roots.

Cultural Learning Series: The Cultural Workshop Series invites survivors to teach traditional skills like regalia making to youth and families, fostering a shared sense of pride and cultural preservation.
